query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticle stability under high‐temperature service regimes is governed by the kinetic trapping of a high-entropy, single-phase solid solution that is achieved by limiting atomic mobility during the synthesis. The resulting severe lattice strain and minimized diffusion pathways hinder phase segregation, thereby preserving both the structural and chemical uniformity of the nanoparticles during operation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized via low-temperature reduction of mixed metal precursors (e.g., those generated from single-source precursors with limited free atom mobility).
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one using the low-temperature, kinetically constrained synthesis method that limits atomic diffusion, and another using a higher-temperature synthesis (or a solution-based method) where atom mobility is greater. Both sets should have identical overall composition.
generation.conditions: Testing performed under catalytic conditions at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operating temperatures up to ~1923 K; nanoparticles should be supported on inert or weakly interacting substrates to isolate intrinsic nanoparticle stability.
generation.structural_mediator: The internal lattice strain induced by atomic size mismatch and the high configurational disorder within the kinetically frozen single-phase nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: During low-temperature synthesis, limited atomic mobility results in a ‘frozen-in’ random alloy configuration in which atoms remain locked into place. The concomitant lattice strain increases the energy barrier for interdiffusion, thereby impeding phase separation or elemental segregation during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles produced via the kinetically constrained, low-temperature method will exhibit a more uniform single-phase solid solution with minimal phase segregation or coarsening during high-temperature operation, compared to nanoparticles obtained from methods with higher atomic mobility. This should be observable as maintained size and compositional uniformity in post-service structural and chemical characterizations.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized under conditions that allow higher atomic mobility (e.g., high-temperature or solution-based processes), which are expected to show partial phase separation or local segregation upon high-temperature treatment.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative primarily in nanoparticles of sufficiently small size (e.g., <10 nm) where the kinetic trapping and strain effects dominate, and within the tested temperature range provided the nanoparticles remain below the melting or sintering thresholds.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the degree of atomic mobility inhibition during synthesis, the magnitude of lattice strain, and the resultant high-temperature stability is not yet fully established and may depend on specific element combinations and particle sizes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of HEA nanoparticles with identical compositions using (a) a low-temperature, kinetic-trapping synthesis method and (b) a higher-temperature/solution-phase synthesis method. Subject both batches to prolonged annealing at 773–1173 K (or thermoelectric operating conditions) under inert atmosphere. Characterize both batches using X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and elemental mapping before and after annealing.
measurements: Phase purity and lattice parameters via XRD
Particle size distribution and morphology via TEM
Elemental homogeneity via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles synthesized by the low-temperature method do not demonstrate significantly improved structural and chemical stability (i.e., maintained single-phase character, particle size, and compositional uniformity) relative to those made by the higher-temperature method, then the hypothesis that kinetic trapping and associated lattice strain govern high-temperature stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways.
